title: Ankara Says It Has a Black Sea Grain Plan and Is in Contact With Russia and Ukraine; Greece and Israel Sign €3B Air Defense Deal
subhead: Turkey moved to revive Black Sea grain exports as wheat prices fell on the news, while a landmark Greece-Israel air defense pact sharpened the eastern Mediterranean rivalry Ankara faces on two fronts.

sections.heading: Black Sea Grain Plan Resurfaces as Ankara Courts Both Sides
sections.body: Turkey says it has a Black Sea grain plan and is in contact with both Russia and Ukraine, according to Reuters. The announcement, reported on August 31, immediately moved markets: Chicago wheat futures fell as traders priced in the possibility of renewed grain flows through the corridor, per TradingView. Ankara has historically positioned itself as the indispensable intermediary on this route, having brokered the original UN-backed grain deal in 2022 before Moscow withdrew. The current push comes amid a broader war economy in which grain transit has been repeatedly disrupted, and it signals Turkey is again trying to carve out a mediating role even as it balances its NATO obligations against its working relationship with Moscow.
sections.whyItMatters: A revived grain corridor would ease global food prices and hand Ankara a concrete diplomatic win, but it depends on both Russia and Ukraine accepting terms — a fragile proposition that has failed before.

sections.heading: Greece and Israel Sign Landmark Air Defense Pact
sections.body: Greece and Israel signed a defense agreement worth over NIS 10 billion (roughly €3 billion) under which Israel will help Greece build an air defense shield, according to AP News and The Jerusalem Post. The deal, reported on August 31, was framed by Israeli and Greek officials as a response to shared threats from Turkey and Iran. Turkish Minute noted the agreement comes amid heightened Turkey-Israel tensions over Syria. The pact deepens a security axis that has been building for years — Greece has hosted Israeli air force exercises and both countries share concerns about Turkish assertiveness in the eastern Mediterranean and Ankara's military presence in Syria.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal hardens the eastern Mediterranean balance against Turkey at a moment when Ankara is simultaneously confronting Israel in Syria and managing Aegean friction with Greece, effectively facing a coordinated southern flank.

sections.heading: Economic Confidence Ticks Above 100 as Rate-Cut Bets Build
sections.body: Türkiye's economic confidence index returned above 100 in August, according to Hürriyet Daily News, a modest signal that households and businesses are less pessimistic than earlier in the year. Separately, Bank of America sees the central bank delivering a single rate cut in October, per Hürriyet Daily News, as the bank weighs easing against an inflation outlook clouded by energy prices. The picture is mixed: confidence is improving, but the war-driven energy shock and a widening trade deficit continue to weigh on the lira and on the central bank's room to move.
sections.whyItMatters: A single, cautious October cut would signal the central bank believes disinflation is on track, but energy costs tied to the regional war remain the key risk to that bet.

sections.heading: Turkey-Israel Rivalry Stays Hot in Syria and the Courts
sections.body: The Turkey-Israel confrontation continued to escalate on multiple tracks. Anadolu Agency reported Ankara slamming Israeli Foreign Ministry remarks targeting President Erdogan, while The New York Times published a broad assessment of the two countries vying for regional influence. The Jerusalem Post quoted an expert warning that Turkey's NATO combat doctrine, combined with its Syria presence, poses a threat to Israel. Ankara has also sought an Interpol notice for Netanyahu in the Gaza flotilla case, per Reuters and Al Jazeera. The rivalry now spans military positioning in Syria, diplomatic attacks, and legal action — a multi-front contest with no sign of de-escalation.
sections.whyItMatters: The dispute has moved beyond rhetoric into concrete military and legal moves, and the new Greece-Israel pact gives Israel a second lever against Turkey in the eastern Mediterranean.

sections.heading: Cyprus Ferry Disaster: Search Continues for 20 Missing
sections.body: Rescue efforts off northern Cyprus continued as a Turkish deep-sea search vessel joined operations to retrieve 20 people still missing after the ferry disaster, according to The Guardian and Al Jazeera. The death toll held at eight, with the number of missing raised to 20. Ankara has mounted a large-scale rescue operation, and Erdogan spoke with Turkish Cypriot leaders as the response continued, per Türkiye Today. The disaster has become a major domestic and humanitarian story for Ankara, which treats the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus as a close ally.
sections.whyItMatters: Beyond the human toll, the disaster tests Ankara's emergency-response capacity and its political commitment to the Turkish Cypriot community at a sensitive moment in Cyprus diplomacy.

sections.heading: SDF Dissolution Reshapes Kurdish Question for Ankara
sections.body: Analysis from RFI examined what the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) means for Syria's Kurds and for neighboring Turkey. The SDF's winding down — a process Ankara has long demanded — removes a key irritant in Turkey's Syria policy but raises new questions about the fate of Kurdish-held areas and the PKK-linked structures Turkey has fought for years. For Ankara, the development is double-edged: it eases the threat on its southern border but leaves a vacuum that could be filled by Damascus, the US, or renewed instability.
sections.whyItMatters: The SDF's dissolution is a strategic shift in northern Syria that Turkey has sought for a decade, but its aftermath — who controls the territory and weapons — will determine whether it is a win or a new problem for Ankara.

bottomLine: Turkey opened the week on two fronts: it floated a revived Black Sea grain plan that moved global wheat prices, and it watched Greece and Israel sign a €3 billion air defense pact aimed squarely at Ankara's regional posture. The grain initiative is a bid to reclaim a mediating role Ankara has struggled to hold, while the Greece-Israel deal hardens the eastern Mediterranean balance against it. Domestically, economic confidence edged above 100 and rate-cut bets are building, but the war-driven energy shock and trade deficit keep the central bank cautious. The Cyprus ferry disaster response and the SDF's dissolution round out a day of incremental but consequential movement across Turkey's foreign and domestic agenda.
sources: Reuters, TradingView, AP News, The Jerusalem Post, Turkish Minute, Hürriyet Daily News, Anadolu Agency, The New York Times, Al Jazeera, The Guardian, RFI, Türkiye Today
